full_judgment:
Md Imman Ali J: These criminal appeals, by leave are directed against the judgment and order dated 25-11-2015 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case Nos. 18994, 18995, 18996, 18997, 18998, 18999, 19000, 19001, 19002 and 19003 of 2014, and judgment and order dated 9-8-2017 passed in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 14617 of 2017 discharging the Rules. 

 3. The relevant facts, for disposal of these appeals are that the complainant-respondent No. 2 in the appeals herein on 21-12-2011 filed 11 separate complaint cases in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Chattogram, stating that the appellant herein issued 11 cheques of Taka 50,00,000 (taka fifty lac) each on 27-6-2011 in favour of respondent No. 2 who presented the cheques for encashment on 28-6-2011, which was dishonoured and the complainant published a legal notice in the Daily Azadi on 14-7-2011. The complainant took no further action under the provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act, but instead represented the cheques on 1-11-2011 for encashment in the Prime Bank Limited, OR Nizam Road Branch, Chattogram which were dishonoured with endorsements 'Account Dormant'. The accused-appellant was informed about the fact and the person concerned working for the complainant company requested him to pay the cheque amounts, but no heed was paid to the request. Thereafter, on 17-11-2011 the Managing Director of the complainant company issued a legal notice and published the same in the 'Daily Jugantor' asking the accused-appellant to pay off the cheques' amounts within 30 (thirty) days from the date of publication. Despite the notice being published as aforesaid the appellant did not pay off the dues. Such failure on the part of the accused amounted to an offence punishable under section 138(1)(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (the Act). The petitions of complaint were filed on 21-12-2011 giving rise to the CR cases sought to be quashed in the High Court Division. 

 I. For that the High Court Division erred in law in discharging the Rules without considering that the proceeding initiated under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 against the accused petitioner is barred by section 141 (1)(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 as the complainant earlier issued legal notice in the 'Daily Azadi on 14-7-2011 for dishonour of the cheques on 28-6-2011 but the complainant without taking recourse to the appropriate remedy within the time fixed under section 141(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 again issued legal notice published in the daily 'Jugantor' on 17-11-2011 for dishonour of self-same cheques on 2-11-2011 and filed the instant case on 21-11-2011 under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 on the basis of second notice published in the daily 'Jugantor' long after the expiry of the period of limitation. 

 5. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali and Mr AM Aminuddin, learned Senior Advocates appearing on behalf of the appellant made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. It was also submitted that having regard to the established principle of law and the ratio decided in the case of 'Motaleb Hossain (Md) vs Abdul Haque Limon & another reported in 21 BLC (AD) 174 to the effect that offence committed and cause of action for an offence punishable under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 arose immediately on the failure by the drawer to make payment within 30 days of the receipt of the notice served in accordance with section 138(1)(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and if the drawee failed to file a case within one month from the date of cause of action arising as prescribed under section 141(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the Courts' power to extend the period of limitation is excluded in view of section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908 as period of limitation for filing complaint under section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 for an offence punishable under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is a special law, as such, the instant complaint filed on 21-12-2011 on the basis of second notice dated 17-11-2011 four months after the cause of action arose, i.e. 14-8-2011, is barred by limitation, consequently the High Court Division erred in law in not considering this vital legal aspect of the matter. It was submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the notice dated 14-7-2011 published in the daily 'Azadi' which being local daily newspaper can by no means be taken as constituting cause of action interpreting the section 138(1A) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 wrongly although the complainant in his affidavit admitted that the notice published in the daily 'Azadi' was served upon the accused and in view of the clear cut admission of service of notice dated 14-7-2011 and receipt of the same, the question of publishing notice in the newspaper is immaterial. Lastly it was submitted that the whole purpose of service of notice by the complainant under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is to allow the drawer some time (30 days) to make arrangement for payment of the dishonoured cheque and in the instant case the accused-petitioner-appellant herein who admittedly received the notice dated 14-7-2011 published in the daily 'Azadi' failed to make payment within 30 days of the receipt of the said notice dated 14-7-2011 hence the cause of action arose on 14-8-2011 as per law but the complainant without filing a complaint under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, within the time fixed by section 141(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which being a special law, again issued notice dated 17-11-2011 published in the daily Jugantor' and initiated the present case long after the period of limitation against the accused-petitioner-appellant herein consequently the High Court Division committed gross error of law in holding that publication of notice in the daily 'Azadi', i.e. notice dated 14-7-2011 being a local daily newspaper can by no means be taken as constituting cause of action without considering this vital legal aspect of the matter. 

 9. The civil liability arising out of dishonour of a cheque or other negotiable instruments is dealt with in chapter VIII of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (the Act). Sections 138 to 141 of the Act were introduced by way of substitution of Chapter XVII of the Act by Act No. XIX of 1994 specifically to deal with the common phenomenon of dishonoured cheques and with a view to compel the drawers of cheques to honour their commitment to pay the amount of money mentioned on the cheque when it is presented for encashment. (Subsequent amendments were made by Act No. XVII of 2000 and Act No. III of 2006). The provisions in those sections give rise to criminal liability with consequent sanctions to be visited upon the party in default to compel him to make payment. It is a strict liability offence, and hence there is no requirement to prove the mens rea or guilty intention of the person drawing the cheque. It will not be a defence on the part of the drawer of the cheque that when he issued the cheque he intended to pay the beneficiary of the cheque and/or that he had sufficient funds in his account when he wrote the cheque. All that is required is for the beneficiary of the cheque to show that the cheque was dishonoured when presented for payment. If, for whatever reason, the cheque is not honoured, then the beneficiary can take action in accordance with the provisions of section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. According to section 138(1) of the Act, the offence is deemed to have been committed by the drawer of the cheque when the cheque is returned by the bank unpaid. However, just as the liability of the drawer of the cheque is strict, so also the conditions detailed in section 138 of the Act must be strictly followed to the letter if the beneficiary of the cheque is to succeed. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provides as follows: "138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc. of funds in the account (1).—Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to thrice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless—(a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of the said notice." 

 12. Sometimes, even before a formal notice is given by the beneficiary of the cheque, the drawer may request that the cheque be placed again for payment. As long as the beneficiary presents the cheque to the bank for payment within the period of six months from the date on which the cheque was drawn, he may still proceed under section 138 of the Act, in case the cheque is again dishonoured. 

 13. It is well settled that a cheque may be presented for payment on any number of occasions, thus on each occasion giving the drawer of the cheque an opportunity to honour his obligation to pay the amount due on the cheque. In the case of Munshi Md Rashed Kamal vs Abdus Salam, 10 BLC (AD) 186 where the cheque had been presented for payment on four occasions, the beneficiary served the required notice after the last dishonour of the cheque, within the statutory period, it was held that there was no illegality 

 (a) no Court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under section 138 except upon a complaint, in writing, made by the payee or, as the case may be, the holder in due course of the cheque; (b) such complaint is made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138; 1(c) no court inferior to that of a Court of Sessions shall try any offence punish-able under section 138.1" 

 18. It has been argued before us that the cause of action arose when upon receiving notice under proviso (b) to section 138(1) the drawer of the cheque failed to make payment within 30 days of receiving notice, and that the cause of action for a dishonoured cheque arises only once. In this regard, reference was made to the case of Nazrul Islam Mallik vs Tofazzal Hossain, 8 BLC 443, where the High Court Division mentioned in passing that the combined reading of sections 138 and 141 leaves no room for doubt that the cause of action within the meaning of section 141(c) arises and can only arise once. The issue in that case was whether a cheque could be presented for payment more than once. That question was answered in the affirmative following the decision of this Division in the case of Habibur Rahman Howlader vs State, 53 DLR (AD) 111. The High Court Division expressed the view that— once on the bouncing of a cheque a notice is served under proviso (b) of section 138(1), the proceeding must be initiated within one month from the date of failure on the part of the drawer to pay the amount within 15 days of the receipt of notice. If after service of notice the drawer fails to pay the amount within 15 days and the payee does not initiate a proceeding within one month therefrom as provided in section 141, the payee forfeits his right to initiate a proceeding under section 138 of the Act." That proposition is correct to the extent that when the cause of action arises the complaint must be made within the time stipulated by the statute, failing which the proceeding for that cause of action shall be barred. However, in the case before the High Court Division the notice demanding payment was issued only once after the cheque had been presented for payment and dishonoured for the third time. Hence, in the case mentioned above, the issue of whether or not cause of action can arise in respect of any cheque more than once was not before the Court. 

 19. In the case of Dr Md Mofizur Rahman vs Md Bashirullah, 55 DLR 630 the High Court Division faced the issue similar to the one raised before us in the instant appeals. In that case, a cheque was drawn on 25-1-2001. It was presented to the bank for payment for the first time on the same date and thereafter on 1-2-2001, 1-4-2001 and lastly on 9-7-2001. On each occasion the cheque was returned uncashed on the date of presentation. The beneficiary of the cheque sent a notice on 8-4-2001, 25-4-2001 and finally on 16-7-2001. The complaint was made on 7-8-2001. The High Court Division held that there cannot be any recurring causes of action and that the case was not filed within the time as required under section 138(b) of the Act read with section 141(b) of the Act since the complaint was not made within the time limit from the date of the first notice on 8-4-2001. 

 20. We note that the High Court Division rightly observed that the cheque in question was first dishonoured on 25-1-2001, whereas the notice under section 138(b) was sent on 8-4-2001 which was beyond the statutory period of limitation. It was, however, within time from the third dishonour on 1-4-2001. The High Court Division held that since the complaint was made according to the provision of section 138(b) of the Act after the cheque was dishonoured for the first time, he could not again avail of the provision of this section after subsequent dishonour of the cheque as in that event sections 138(c) and 141(b) of the Act would become nugatory. We note also that the learned Advocate appearing for the accused in that case referred to the decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Sadanandan Bhadran vs Madhavan Sunil Kumar, AIR 1998 SC 3043 in which it had been held that:  cause of action under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act arises and can arise only once. Payee can present cheque any number of times during the period of its validity and on each presentation and its dishonour a fresh right, and not cause of action, accrues in his favour." 

 21. No doubt, the High Court Division was swayed by the decision of the Indian Supreme Court and the above quotation which was reproduced in the judgement. It must be noted, however, that the case of Sadanandan Bhadran was overruled by the Supreme Court of India by its later judgment dated 26-9-2012 in the case of MSR Leathers vs S. Palaniappan, (2013) 1 SCC 117. 

 22. In the Sadanandan case the Supreme Court of India had held that the language of sections 138 and 142 (which is similar to our section 141) clearly postulates only one cause of action. It was observed that for dishonour of one cheque, there can be only one offence and such offence is committed by the drawer immediately on his failure to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of the notice served in accordance with clause (b) of the proviso to section 138. However, when dealing with the case of MSR Leathers, their Lordships reviewed their own position and observed, "What is important is that neither Section 138 nor section 142 or any other provision contained in the Act forbids the holder or payee of the cheque from presenting the cheque for encashment on any number of occasions within a period of six months of its issue or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier". Their Lordships further observed, 

 25. The moot point in the cases before us is as to whether the beneficiary of a cheque, who does not lodge a complaint after issuing a legal notice upon dishonour of a cheque, can present the cheque for payment again and upon subsequent dishonour issue another legal notice and file a complaint thereafter. The answer must be in the affirmative since the law allows the beneficiary of the cheque to present the same for payment any number of times within a period of six months from the date it is drawn and gives him the right to make a complaint when the cheque is dishonoured, as long as he does so within the period stipulated in the statute. 

 26. It is our considered view that there is no conflict between proviso (c) to section 138(1) and section 141(b). Sections 138 and 140 of the Act are substantive provisions of law giving details of the offence, when the offence is committed and who is liable; section 141 of the Act describes the procedure to be followed. The intention of the legislature in enacting section 141(b) is to provide a time limit within which the complaint against the defaulting drawer of the cheque is to be made. This section does not preclude the holder of the cheque from presenting the cheque to the bank again for payment, subject only to the condition that the second and subsequent presentation of the cheque must be within six months from the date on which the cheque was drawn in order to be able to prosecute the drawer of the cheque criminally under section 138 of the Act. Upon subsequent presentation of the cheque for payment, if it is again dishonoured another opportunity will accrue to the beneficiary to take action as provided under section 138(1) of the Act, and again, in accordance with the provisions of section 141, the beneficiary of the cheque will be obliged to make complaint against such subsequent dishonour within a period of one month from the cause of action arising under proviso (c) to section 138(1) of the Act. The offence is committed each time the cheque is dishonoured on presentation for payment. There is nothing in section 141(b) to suggest that the cause of action cannot arise more than once under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138(1). The procedural limitation provided in section 141(b) cannot take away the substantive right accruing to the beneficiary of a cheque to prosecute any number of subsequent presentation of the cheque on its dishonour. Similarly, each dishonour will give rise to a concomitant right to serve notice under proviso (b) to section 138(1) of the Act and demand payment, failing which the bearer of the cheque will have the right to make a complaint in writing in accordance with section 141(a) of the Act. It will be entirely up to the bearer of the cheque to proceed in respect of any particular dishonour of the cheque, keeping in mind that each step of the process has to be taken within the period stipulate by the law. Hence, we hold that decision in the case of Dr Md Mofizur Rahman vs Md Bashirullah, 55 DLR 630 was incorrect and is accordingly overruled.
